reverseBrief.humanQuestion: When reports show women hired into AI jobs and using AI daily less often than men, does that mean women are less interested or capable — or that employers distribute access unevenly?

explainBack.question: Why can the Census finding that 30% of men but 17% of women use AI daily at work not be read as evidence that women are less able or less interested in AI?
explainBack.answer: Because how often someone uses AI depends heavily on conditions her employer controls: whether she was given an approved tool, paid time to learn it, and an invitation to a project where it is used. Two equally interested colleagues with different conditions will show different usage. On top of that, if managers pick trial teams only from existing users, early access differences compound, so a frequency gap can grow without any difference in ability. The survey also only measures self-reported frequency among people who already used AI — it never measured skill, interest or access at all.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer should cite the conditions mechanism (tool, paid time, invitation) from P006, the compounding selection effect from P007, and the measurement limits from P003–P004 (different populations; frequency is not ability).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this answer: P006 supplies the conditions mechanism with an explicit epistemic boundary, P007 supplies the compounding step, and P004 supplies the measurement limits, all in ordinary language.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A regional hospital introduces an AI note-summarising assistant. After three months, dashboards show day-shift administrative staff logging in far more than night-shift nurses. The operations director proposes staffing the permanent rollout committee with the ten heaviest users, and a board member suggests the login gap shows nurses 'aren't interested in AI'.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, what should the director check before treating the login gap as a preference or ability gap, and how should the committee be selected?
unseenTransfer.answer: First check the conditions: night nurses may have had no scheduled paid time to learn the tool, restricted terminals, or no invitation to the pilot — so their lower logins may reflect access, not interest. Second, avoid the compounding step: selecting the committee only from heavy users would hand a further opportunity to whoever had early access, entrenching the gap. Instead, publish visible selection criteria, include a supported route for non-users (training time within their shift workload), and judge success by useful work and sound judgment rather than a daily-usage target.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: The answer should apply P006's conditions test, P007's warning about selecting only existing users, and P009–P010's visible criteria, supported route and non-usage-based success measure to this new hospital setting.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism transfers cleanly and completely to this unseen scenario; every step of the answer follows from P006, P007, P009 and P010 without needing information the article lacks.
